partial_case.facts: The resident lives in a flat with their young child. At the time the landlord was investigating this complaint, the resident was pregnant. On 2 May 2025, the resident complained to the landlord that no one had turned up to a pre-arranged appointment to address the damp and mould in their property. The condition of the property was worsening, and there was now fungal growth in the property. They were concerned about the impact of the conditions, as they were pregnant, had asthma, and had experienced regular asthma attacks. The landlord sent its stage one response on 16 June 2025, acknowledging it was unaware that its contractors had failed to attend the 2 May 2025 appointment until the resident complained. It was attempting to re-book the appointment and offered compensation of £50 for poor communication, £25 for the missed appointment, and £150 for inconvenience, time and trouble. On 25 June 2025, the resident escalated their complaint as they were concerned about the worsening conditions and the potential impact this could have on their pregnancy. The landlord sent its stage 2 response on 31 July 2025, stating it had been notified of the damp and mould on 24 March 2025 and opened a case on 27 March 2025. It summarised delays including contractor non-attendance, the case being closed, unsuccessful contact efforts, and rescheduled appointments. A damp and mould wash had not yet occurred, with an appointment scheduled for 18 August 2025. It offered additional compensation of £50 for failure to make reasonable adjustments and £200 for inconvenience, bringing total compensation to £475.

claim_types: Landlord's handling of damp and mould in the property
evidence: Resident's complaint and escalation correspondence about damp, mould, missed appointments, health concerns, and pregnancy.
Landlord's stage one and stage two complaint responses, including compensation offers and explanations for delay.
Landlord policies on damp and mould, repairs, rehousing, and complaints timescales.
Damp and mould survey evidence identifying mould in all rooms and recommendations for remedial works.
partial_case.facts: The resident lives in a flat with their young child and was pregnant when the landlord was investigating the complaint. The complaint concerned the landlord's handling of damp and mould in the property, and complaint handling was also considered. On 2 May 2025 the resident complained to the landlord, saying no one had attended a pre-arranged appointment about damp and mould, the property condition was worsening, there was fungal growth, and they were pregnant, had asthma, and had experienced regular asthma attacks. On 16 June 2025 the landlord sent its stage one response, saying it had been unaware contractors failed to attend until the complaint, was attempting to re-book the appointment, apologised for the delay, acknowledged the resident was pregnant, and offered compensation of £50, £25, and £150. On 25 June 2025 the resident escalated the complaint because of worsening conditions and the potential impact on pregnancy, and wanted the property brought to a liveable standard. On 31 July 2025 the landlord sent its stage 2 response, stating it had been notified of damp and mould on 24 March 2025 and opened a damp and mould case on 27 March 2025, and identifying delays including contractor non-attendance, closure of the damp and mould case, unsuccessful contact efforts, and rescheduled appointments. The stage 2 response said a damp and mould wash had not yet occurred, an appointment was scheduled for 18 August 2025, and after the wash the landlord would consider temporary rehousing due to the resident's vulnerabilities. The landlord offered further compensation at stage 2, bringing the total compensation offered by the landlord to £475. On 1 August 2025 the resident contacted the Ombudsman again and said they were extremely stressed, felt the landlord was not helping them, and said the stress was impacting their health and ability to prepare for their baby's arrival.

determinations: Maladministration in the landlord's handling of damp and mould in the property
Service failure in the landlord's complaints handling
orders: Landlord to pay the resident £550 compensation, made up of £500 for distress and concern associated with ongoing damp and mould issues and £50 for inconvenience associated with complaint handling.
Landlord to arrange a damp and mould survey by a suitably qualified professional with a written report shared with the resident.
Landlord to produce a schedule of repairs following the survey.
Landlord to provide a plan for temporary rehousing if planned repairs cannot be completed in line with repairs policy timescales.

key_reasoning_quotes.text: The landlord has not adequately addressed the damp and mould in the property, and the issues have been ongoing for a significant period.
When a landlord becomes aware of vulnerability, we expect it to assess the risk and prioritise actions if necessary. There is no evidence this occurred.
The landlord did not arrange temporary rehousing despite the resident requesting it, and we have seen no evidence to suggest it considered this option following the mould wash.

Given that the damp and mould issues have not been resolved, the works identified in the last survey have not been progressed, and the resident’s concerns that there could be other factors contributing to the situation, it would be appropriate for the landlord to carry out a further inspection.
We have found a service failure occurred as the resident experienced delays at stage one, and the landlord did not acknowledge or apologise for the delay.
